chapters.title: Chapter 3: Debt Funds, Bonds and Gold

lessons.title: Listed Bonds, Unlisted Bonds, Zero-Coupon Bonds and Market-Linked Debentures

body.text: A bond can pay you in two ways: interest while you hold it, and a price gain or loss when you sell or it matures. The tax law treats these separately, and whether the bond is listed can decide whether your gain is taxed at 12.5% or at your full slab rate.

children.text: Farhan, a 45-year-old operations head in Mumbai, has four kinds of fixed income. He bought listed NCDs of an NBFC on Zerodha, an unlisted corporate bond through an online bond platform, a market-linked debenture pitched by his relationship manager, and his father handed him NHAI tax-free bonds bought in 2016. He assumed "bonds are bonds" for tax. They are not.

columns.label: Interest (Coupon)
points: Taxed as income from other sources at your slab rate
Taxable in the year it is received or accrues
TDS at 10% on listed debenture interest above the annual threshold
Fully exempt only for notified tax-free bonds such as older NHAI, REC, PFC and IRFC issues

columns.label: Capital Gain or Loss
points: Arises when you sell the bond or it is redeemed at maturity
Sale or redemption value minus your purchase cost
Short-term or long-term depends on listing status and holding period
Some bonds are deemed short-term no matter how long you hold them

body.title: Which Bond Can Give a 12.5% Gain?
body.question: Farhan has held each of these for three years. Which one can give a long-term capital gain taxed at 12.5% if he sells now at a profit?
options: An unlisted corporate bond bought through a bond platform
A listed market-linked debenture linked to the Nifty 50
A listed NCD bought on NSE
All three, because each has been held for more than 24 months
body.explanation: Only the listed NCD qualifies. Unlisted bonds are deemed short-term for transfers from 23 July 2024, and MLDs, listed or not, are deemed short-term from 1 April 2023. Both are taxed at slab rate however long they are held.

children.text: Listed bonds run on the 12-month clock from Chapter 1. Farhan bought 100 listed NCDs with a face value of ₹1,000 and a 9% annual coupon at ₹980 each in August 2024. Every year he receives ₹9,000 of interest, taxed at his 30% slab: ₹2,700 before cess. In September 2026 he sells all 100 on NSE at ₹1,015 each.

body.title: Farhan's NCD Gain
body.prompt: Farhan bought 100 listed NCDs at ₹980 each in August 2024 and sold them at ₹1,015 each in September 2026. Ignoring expenses and accrued interest, what is his capital gain in rupees?
body.explanation: Gain = 100 × (₹1,015 − ₹980) = ₹3,500. He held them for more than 12 months, so this is long-term and taxed at 12.5% under section 197: ₹437.5 before cess. There is no ₹1.25 lakh exemption, which applies only to listed equity.

body.text: Holding to maturity counts too. If Farhan had bought at ₹980 and held until the issuer repaid ₹1,000 face value, the ₹20 per NCD would be a capital gain on redemption, long-term if held for more than 12 months.

body.title: How the Deemed Short-Term Net Widened

events.title: MLDs sold as "tax-efficient"
events.description: Listed MLDs held for more than 12 months were taxed at 10% as long-term gains, far below the 30% slab many high-income buyers faced. They became a popular product for exactly that reason.

events.title: MLDs become deemed short-term
events.description: Gains on market-linked debentures, listed or unlisted, became short-term irrespective of holding period, taxed at slab rates.

events.title: Unlisted bonds join them
events.description: Gains on unlisted bonds and unlisted debentures transferred, redeemed or maturing on or after this date became deemed short-term too.

events.title: Section 76 of the Income-tax Act, 2025
events.description: Both rules continue under section 76 of the new Act (section 50AA of the 1961 Act).

markDefs.definition: A debenture whose return is not fixed but depends on the performance of an underlying market variable such as an equity index. Gains are deemed short-term capital gains since 1 April 2023, whether listed or unlisted.

children.text: pays a return linked to something like the Nifty 50 rather than a fixed coupon. Many investors bought them before April 2023 precisely because of the 10% long-term rate. That advantage is gone.

body.context: Tax before cess on a ₹40,000 gain from selling 10 unlisted bonds bought at ₹1,00,000 and sold at ₹1,04,000 each. Had the same bond been listed, the long-term tax would have been ₹5,000.

body.title: The MLD Rule
body.textWithBlank: Gains on market-linked debentures, listed or unlisted, are always treated as short-term and taxed at your ___ rate.
body.explanation: Since 1 April 2023, MLD gains are deemed short-term under what is now section 76 of the 2025 Act, so they are added to your income and taxed at your slab rate regardless of how long you hold them.

children.text: A zero-coupon bond pays no interest. You buy it at a discount and receive face value at maturity, so your entire return is the difference. For a listed or notified zero-coupon bond, that difference is a capital gain. Buy 20 at ₹7,500 and receive ₹10,000 each three years later, and your gain is ₹50,000, long-term after more than 12 months and taxed at 12.5%: ₹6,250 before cess.

body.title: Deep Dive: Deep Discount Bonds and Accrued Interest

children.text: Not every bond issued at a discount is a zero-coupon bond for tax. Deep discount bonds that are not notified as zero-coupon bonds have historically been taxed differently, with the discount treated as interest that accrues over the life of the bond. Check the offer document and the issuer's stated tax treatment before assuming capital gains treatment.

When you buy a coupon-paying bond between interest dates on the exchange, you usually pay the seller the interest accrued since the last coupon on top of the clean price. When you sell, you receive accrued interest from the buyer. How that accrued interest is split between interest income and capital gain can affect your figures. Your broker's contract note separates clean price and accrued interest, so keep it.
Tax-Free Bonds: Tax-Free Interest, Taxable Gains

Tax-free bonds issued by NHAI, REC, PFC, IRFC and similar entities, mostly between 2011 and 2016, pay interest that is fully exempt. They still trade on NSE and BSE, and when interest rates fall, their prices rise. Selling at a profit gives an ordinary capital gain on a listed bond.

body.title: Should Farhan Sell His Father's Tax-Free Bonds?
body.scenario: Farhan now holds 200 NHAI tax-free bonds his father bought in 2016 at ₹1,000 face value. The bonds pay tax-free interest and trade on NSE at ₹1,120. Farhan is in the 30% slab and is tempted to sell and move the money into a 9% listed NCD.
body.prompt: What tax would he pay on selling, and what should he weigh before switching?
body.modelAnswer: The bonds came to him from his father, so his holding period includes his father's since 2016 and his cost is his father's ₹1,000 per bond. Gain = 200 × (₹1,120 − ₹1,000) = ₹24,000, long-term, taxed at 12.5%: ₹3,000 before cess. Before switching, he should compare post-tax yields. A 9% taxable NCD gives him about 6.3% after 30% tax, while his tax-free bond's interest is untouched by tax. He should also compare credit risk, since an NBFC NCD is riskier than an NHAI bond, and the fact that new tax-free bond issues are rare, so he may not be able to buy back in later.

cards.definition: Periodic interest on a bond. Taxed at slab rate unless the bond is notified tax-free.
Long-term after more than 12 months. LTCG at 12.5% under section 197, no exemption.
Deemed short-term for transfers or maturity from 23 July 2024. Slab rate.
Market-linked debenture. Deemed short-term since 1 April 2023, listed or unlisted.
Bought at a discount, redeemed at face value. The discount is a capital gain.
Interest exempt, but gains on sale are taxable like any listed bond.

body.title: Sort Your Fixed Income Holdings
steps: List every bond, NCD, MLD and tax-free bond you hold, and mark each as listed or unlisted
Check the offer document or platform listing to confirm whether a product is an MLD
Record each purchase price, date and any accrued interest paid from your contract notes
Match TDS on interest in your AIS against the coupons you actually received
For unlisted bonds and MLDs, estimate tax on any gain at your slab rate before selling
Compare post-tax yields, not headline coupons, before switching between bonds

points: Bond interest is taxed at slab rate every year; only notified tax-free bonds escape it
Listed bonds and NCDs become long-term after more than 12 months and are taxed at 12.5%, with no ₹1.25 lakh exemption
Unlisted bonds and debentures are deemed short-term for transfers or maturity from 23 July 2024
Market-linked debentures have been deemed short-term since 1 April 2023, listed or unlisted
A zero-coupon bond's entire return is a capital gain, long-term after more than 12 months
Tax-free bonds give exempt interest, but selling them at a profit is still a taxable capital gain
